stem: Which basis is most suitable for apportioning the rent of a shop among its departments?

options.content: Floor area used by each department
options.rationale: Correct: the rent pays for space.

options.content: Number of customers who enter the shop
options.rationale: Customers do not determine the rent.

options.content: Sales of each department in the year
options.rationale: Sales do not show how much space is used.
Purchases are not linked to the space occupied.

explanation: Rent buys space, so the fair basis is the floor area of each department.

stem: Which basis is most suitable for apportioning general staff wages that serve all departments?

options.content: The number of staff in each department
options.rationale: Correct: more staff in a department means more staff costs.

options.content: The floor area of each department
options.rationale: Space has no link to the number of staff.

options.content: The value of assets used in each department
options.rationale: Assets do not determine staff costs.
Departments with more staff would be undercharged.

explanation: General staff wages are best shared by the number of staff in each department, as that reflects who uses staff services.

stem: Commission received by a business as a whole from a supplier is:

options.rationale: It is income, not an expense.

options.content: added to the department with the highest sales only
options.rationale: It is shared on a suitable basis.
It increases total profit, so it must be shown.

options.content: ancillary income, shared among the departments
options.rationale: Correct: it is not earned by one department alone.

explanation: Income that is not earned by one department alone is shared on a suitable basis, usually sales.

stem: Rent of US\$18,000 is apportioned on floor area. Department A occupies 150 m², B occupies 100 m² and C occupies 50 m². How much rent is charged to department B?

options.rationale: That is the share of department A.
That is the share of department C.
The total floor area has been taken as 150 m² instead of 300 m².

stem: General wages of US\$15,200 are apportioned by the number of staff: department A has 4 staff, B has 3 and C has 1. What is charged to department A?

options.rationale: The wages have been shared equally among three departments.
That is the share of department B.
The total number of staff is 8, not 3.

stem: A business changes the basis on which rent is apportioned from sales to floor area. What is the effect on the total profit of the business?

options.rationale: The total rent is unchanged.

options.content: No effect; only the split between departments changes
options.rationale: Correct: the same total rent is charged.
The total rent is unchanged.

options.content: Total profit is shown only in the largest department's column
options.rationale: Total profit is the sum of the departmental profits.

explanation: Apportionment only divides a fixed total, so the total profit is the same.

stem: Department X has 2 of the 8 employees and makes 30% of the total sales. General staff wages are US\$24,000 and advertising is US\$10,000, apportioned on staff numbers and on sales respectively. What is the total charge to X for these two expenses?

options.rationale: The bases have been swapped.
A single ratio has been used for both expenses.
The sales ratio has been used for both expenses.

hints: Use the staff ratio for wages and the sales ratio for advertising.

stem: Which of these expenses should NOT be apportioned among departments?

options.content: Rent of the whole shop building and yard
options.rationale: It is a common expense and is apportioned.

options.content: The wages of staff who work only in one department
options.rationale: Correct: it is allocated directly to that department.

options.content: Insurance of the whole stock held in the whole shop building
options.rationale: It is a common expense and is apportioned.

options.content: Bank charges of the business as a whole
options.rationale: It is a common expense and is apportioned.

explanation: An expense that clearly belongs to one department is allocated to it directly; common expenses are apportioned.
hints: Which expense belongs clearly to one department?

stem: Changing the basis of apportionment changes the total profit of the business.
explanation: False. The total profit is the same; only the share allocated to each department changes.

stem: Departmental accounts are part of the Cambridge 9706 syllabus.
explanation: False. Departmental accounts are examined by ZIMSEC only.

stem: Match each expense to the most suitable basis of apportionment.
explanation: Each basis follows the way the expense is caused or the benefit received.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: An expense charged wholly to one department is {{blank:a}}. A common expense shared among departments is {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Allocation charges a cost directly; apportionment shares a common cost.

stem: Name the type of income, such as commission received, that is earned by the whole business and shared among the departments.
explanation: Income not earned by one department alone is called ancillary income.

stem: Lighting costs of US\$7,800 are apportioned on floor area. The floor areas are 210 m² (clothing), 130 m² (shoes) and 60 m² (toys). Calculate the lighting cost charged to toys.
Advertising of US\$4,860 is apportioned on sales. Sales were US\$38,000 (clothing), US\$52,000 (shoes) and US\$30,000 (toys). Calculate the advertising charged to shoes.
Commission received of US\$3,900 is shared on sales. Department A had sales of US\$60,000 and department B had sales of US\$70,000. Calculate the commission credited to department A.
Distinguish between allocation and apportionment of expenses.

points.description: Allocation charges an expense wholly to the department that incurred it
Apportionment shares a common expense among departments on a suitable basis

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Allocation charges an expense wholly to one department. Apportionment shares a common expense among departments using a basis such as floor area.

explanation: One mark for each term.

stem: Explain why floor area is a better basis than sales for apportioning rent.

points.description: Rent is paid for the use of space
A department that occupies more space benefits more and should bear more of the cost
A sales basis could undercharge a large department with low sales and overcharge a small one with high sales

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rent pays for space, so a department using more space should carry more of it. Sales does not reflect space and could undercharge a large, slow department.

explanation: One mark for each point.

stem: State three limitations of apportioning common expenses among departments.

points.description: Any basis is a judgement and may not reflect the actual use
Different bases give different departmental profits, so the results can be manipulated
Some common costs, such as the owner's salary, cannot be linked to departments reliably

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Any basis is a judgement. Different bases give different departmental profits. Some costs cannot be linked reliably to departments.

explanation: One mark for each limitation.
hints: Think about how arbitrary a basis can be.

stem: A manager says department C makes a loss only because it is charged rent on floor area, and wants the rent shared on sales instead. Evaluate the suggestion.

points.description: Department C uses a large floor area, so floor area measures its use of the space
Changing to sales would shift rent to other departments and make C look better but would not change the total profit
The change would hide the cost of the space that C uses and could lead to wrong decisions about it
Judgement: keep floor area for rent; consider whether C could use less space or earn more per square metre

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Floor area reflects the space C uses. A sales basis would make C look better by moving rent to other departments, but the total profit would not change. The manager should keep the floor-area basis and consider using less space or earning more per square metre.

explanation: One mark each for the logic of floor area, the effect of the change, the risk of a wrong decision and a judgement.
hints: Does the change affect total profit?

stem:
Shamva Hardware and Paints has two departments, hardware and paints. The common expenses for the year are shown below with the bases of apportionment.

| Expense | US\$ | Basis | Hardware | Paints |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Rent | 14,400 | Floor area (m²) | 180 | 60 |
| Lighting | 2,800 | Floor area (m²) | 180 | 60 |
| General wages | 12,600 | Staff | 4 | 3 |
| Advertising | 4,500 | Sales (US\$) | 63,000 | 27,000 |
| Depreciation | 5,400 | Asset values (US\$) | 30,000 | 15,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rent charged to paints.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the general wages charged to hardware.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation charged to paints.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the total of the common expenses charged to hardware.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State one reason for using asset values to apportion depreciation.

points.description: Depreciation arises on the assets, so departments holding more assets should bear more of the charge

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Depreciation is caused by the assets, so the department with more assets should bear more.

parts.explanation: One mark for the link between depreciation and the assets.

explanation: This item tests the apportionment of five common expenses between two departments.
hints: Find the total of each basis first.
Add the five shares for hardware.

stem:
Gweru Gifts and Books has three departments. The gross profit of each department is: gifts US\$41,500, crafts US\$28,300 and books US\$19,200. The expenses for the year are:

| Item | US\$ | Basis |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Departmental wages (gifts / crafts / books) | 6,200 / 5,400 / 4,100 | Allocated directly |
| Rent | 15,600 | Floor area: 130 / 80 / 50 m² |
| General staff wages | 17,400 | Staff: 5 / 4 / 3 |
| Advertising | 6,480 | Sales: US\$102,000 / 66,000 / 48,000 |
| Commission received (income) | 2,160 | Sales |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rent charged to books.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the general staff wages charged to crafts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total of rent, general staff wages and advertising charged to gifts.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the net profit or loss of books. Enter a loss as a negative number.
parts.explanation: Gross profit 19,200 + commission 480 - wages 4,100 - rent 3,000 - general wages 4,350 - advertising 1,440 = 6,790.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Gross profit 19,200 + commission 480 - wages 4,100 - rent 3,000 - general wages 4,350 - advertising 1,440 = 6,790.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Books shows a lower net profit than the other departments. Evaluate whether this proves that the books department should be closed.

points.description: Books has a net result of 6,790 (compared with 18,210 for gifts), so on these figures it contributes least
The common costs charged to books (rent, general wages, advertising) would remain if it closed, so total profit could fall even more
The result depends on the bases chosen: a different basis could change books' result
Judgement: do not close on this evidence alone; compare books' gross profit with the direct costs it causes, and consider customers it attracts to other departments

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Books has a net result of 6,790, less than the other departments. But most of the common costs charged to it would continue if it closed, and the bases are judgements. The directors should look at its contribution after direct costs, and at the customers it brings in, before deciding.

parts.explanation: One mark each for the comparison with figures, the common costs, the effect of the basis and a judgement.

explanation: This item tests apportionment and the analysis of departmental results.
hints: Compute each department's share of each basis.
